title: Most Frequent Characters First
statement:
You get a string s of letters and digits. Rearrange it so that characters that occur more often come first, with all copies of the same character next to each other. Return the result.

Uppercase and lowercase letters are different characters. When two characters occur equally often, either may come first: any valid order is accepted.

examples.why: a occurs 3 times, n twice and b once. Here the order is fully decided.
b leads with 2. A and a are different characters with one copy each, so "bbaA" is accepted too.
x and y tie with 2 each, so "yyxx9" is also fine. "xyxy9" is not: copies of a character must stay together.

constraints: s contains English letters and digits
hints: First, how often does each character occur? Then the order of the groups is the only thing left to decide.
Sorting the distinct characters by count works and is cheap, since there are at most 62 of them. Can you avoid sorting entirely?
Counts range from 1 to n. Put each character into a bucket indexed by its count, then walk the buckets from n down to 1 and write each character count times.

explain.intuition:
The answer is decided by the counts alone: build a group of count copies for every distinct character and line the groups up from largest to smallest. So the work is counting (one pass with a map) and then ordering the distinct characters by count.

Sorting the distinct characters is fine here, since there are at most 62 of them. The classic trick to skip comparisons entirely is bucket sort: a count can only be between 1 and n, so make an array of n + 1 buckets, drop each character into the bucket for its count, and read the buckets from high to low. That is O(n) for any alphabet size. Build the result with an array join or a list of parts, not by repeated string concatenation in a loop.
steps: Count every character in a map.
Create buckets 0..n. For each character, push it into buckets[count].
Walk the buckets from n down to 1. For each character in a bucket, append it count times to the output.
Join the output and return it.
pitfalls: Sorting the characters of s by count only. Two characters with the same count then end up interleaved, like "xyxy", instead of grouped.
Treating uppercase and lowercase as the same letter.
Building the string with += inside a loop over 500 000 characters in a language where strings are immutable and the engine cannot optimize it.

solutions.title: Count, then sort the distinct characters
solutions.idea: Count with a map, sort the distinct characters by count descending, and repeat each one count times.
solutions.time: O(n + k log k), k distinct characters

solutions.title: Bucket sort by count
solutions.idea: Counts are between 1 and n, so put each character into the bucket for its count and read buckets from high to low. No comparison sort needed.

followups: Break ties by putting the character that appears first in s first. What changes?
Return only the k most frequent characters. Is a heap better than bucket sort here?
